newsitem.title: Australia: Australia bond yields rise ahead of wages verdict.
newsitem.headline: Australia bond yields rise ahead of wages verdict.

text.p: *Australian bond yields ended higher as futures selling took the heat out of last week's strong rally ahead of the upcoming crucial wage and prices reports.
*AIRC verdict due at 2.00 p.m. (0400 GMT) Tuesday.
Australian bond yields finished higher as futures selling took the heat out of last week's strong rally ahead of this week's crucial wage and prices data.

Tuesday will see the release of the long-awaited verdict on the "living wage" claim by the Australian Industrial Relations Commissions (AIRC) at 2.00 p.m. (0400 GMT) followed by the March quarter CPI on Wednesday.
"Good outcomes in both these figures will rekindle speculation about divergent monetary policy between Australia and the U.S.," said Glenn Maguire, economist at Societe Generale.

Economists are expecting the AIRC to hand down a pay award of around A$12 per week, which is not seen having an undue impact on future wages growth and keep average weekly earnings between the Reserve Bank's 4.0 to 4.5 percent comfort zone.
This would be a compromise between the government's A$8 per week and the Australian Council of Trade Unions' A$20 per week and 8.75 percent minimum pay award.
The RBA has warned that a decision that pushed wages growth to a rate inconsistent with its 2.0-3.0 percent underlying inflation target would see it take the approriate monetary policy action.
A higher pay award of A$15 per week or more would also overshadow any positive implications for the bond market from the expected benign outcome in Wednesday's inflation report.

Median forecasts for the headline CPI centre on a rise of just 0.1 percent for an annual rate of 1.2 percent and the underlying rate up 0.4 percent for 2.1 percent annually, according to a Reuters survey of economists.

Anticipation of market-positive outcomes to the wage and inflation data saw the bond and bill futures markets rally strongly last week amid some speculation that the RBA could ease policy again to keep the current patchy recovery in motion.
Traders said today's easier trend was primarily futures selling linked to the purchase of semi-government bonds.
"People are hedging their semis exposure. Semi spreads have come in and TCV (Treasury Corp of Victoria) has met a strong bid," one trader said.

He linked the buying to the imminent sell of the Victorian state's Loy Yang A power station, which sources close to the bidding believe has been won by a consortium led U.S. uitilities NRG Energy Inc and CMS Energy Corp.
The prospect of a sale to an offshore entity, which has been rumoured at A$4.5 billion, also lifted the Australian dollar.

The weaker tone saw the market underperform the bloc and give up almost all the spread narrowing seen last week. In contrast to Australia, U.S. Treasuries face a thin calendar of major data, although it will see US$17 billion of two-year notes and A$12.5 billion of five-year notes auctioned this week.
